:::{#thm-huffman-optimal}
#### Huffman codes are optimal

Let $X$ be a [discrete random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-discrete-rv)
that takes $n \ge 2$ values,
each with [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $p(x) > 0$.
Then a [Huffman code](#def-huffman-code) for $X$
has the least [expected length](source-coding.qmd#def-expected-length) $L$
among all [prefix codes](#def-prefix-code) for $X$.

:::

::: {.proof}

We use [induction](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/proof-writing.html#def-proof-by-induction) on $n$.
For $n = 2$,
every [prefix code](#def-prefix-code) gives each value a codeword of at least one [bit](entropy.qmd#def-bit),
and the [Huffman code](#def-huffman-code) gives them the codewords $0$ and $1$,
so no prefix code is shorter.

Let $n > 2$,
and suppose the claim holds for $n - 1$ values.
Let $x$ and $y$ be two values with the smallest [probabilities](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability),
the pair that the first step of the construction merges.

First, some prefix code with the least [expected length](source-coding.qmd#def-expected-length) has $x$ and $y$ as siblings,
meaning that their codewords have the same length $m$
and differ only in the last bit.
To see this, take a prefix code with the least expected length.

- If $p(u) > p(v)$,
  then $\ell(u) \le \ell(v)$.
  Otherwise, exchanging the codewords of $u$ and $v$
  changes $L$ by $(p(u) - p(v))(\ell(v) - \ell(u)) < 0$.
- A longest codeword $c$ has a sibling.
  Otherwise,
  deleting the last bit of $c$ leaves a string
  that neither begins another codeword nor is begun by one,
  which gives a prefix code with a smaller $L$.

Let $u$ be a value with a longest codeword,
and let $v$ be the value of its sibling.
Both codewords have length $m$,
the largest [codeword length](source-coding.qmd#def-code).
By the first bullet,
exchanging the codeword of $x$ with that of $u$ does not increase $L$,
because $p(x) \le p(u)$ and $\ell(u) = m$ is the largest length.
The same holds for exchanging $y$ with $v$.
If $x$ or $y$ is already one of $u$ and $v$,
leave it where it is,
and exchange the other with the remaining one of the pair.
If $x = v$ and $y \ne u$, for example,
exchange $y$ with $u$.
Ties among the smallest probabilities do not matter,
because every value other than $x$ and $y$ has probability at least $p(y)$,
and the exchanges use only that.
These exchanges give a prefix code with the least expected length
in which $x$ and $y$ are siblings.

Next, let $X'$ be the [random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-random-variable)
that merges $x$ and $y$ into one value $z$ with $p'(z) = p(x) + p(y)$
and keeps every other value and probability.
Any prefix code for $X$ in which $x$ and $y$ are siblings
turns into a prefix code for $X'$
by deleting the last bit of their common codeword to make the codeword of $z$.
The two codes differ only in the lengths of $x$, $y$ and $z$,
so their expected lengths satisfy

$$L = L' + p(x) + p(y).$$

The Huffman code for $X$ is built from a Huffman code for $X'$
by replacing the codeword of $z$ with two codewords,
one that ends in $0$ and one that ends in $1$.
By the induction hypothesis,
a Huffman code for $X'$ has the least expected length $L'$ among prefix codes for $X'$.
So no prefix code for $X$ in which $x$ and $y$ are siblings
has an expected length below that of the Huffman code for $X$.
By the first part,
a prefix code with the least expected length is among these,
so the Huffman code has the least expected length among all prefix codes.

:::
